title: multi-gpu-serving-design-kernels-scheduling-kv-cache
content:
Context and purpose:
This is a working design doc for multi-GPU serving in the Redwood runtime. Focus areas: tensor & pipeline parallelism topology, NCCL tuning and topology-aware collective configs, model & KV-cache sharding, kernel selection strategies, and scheduler changes required to support high-throughput, low-latency inference across multi-GPU nodes. Goal is to converge on a pragmatic design that supports common production models (up to ~70B parameters) with predictable latency SLOs and graceful degradation under resource pressure.

Goals and constraints:
- Throughput: maximize tokens/sec for batched workloads.
- Latency SLO: 95th p99 targets specified per-customer; must avoid high tail caused by pipeline bubbles or oversized all-reduces.
- Memory: support mixed-precision (fp16/amp) and quantized paths; ensure KV cache fits per-GPU partitioning.
- Robustness: tolerant to single-GPU failure within node; graceful fallback to smaller parallelism or single-GPU for degraded availability.
- Operational simplicity: reasonable default configs that work across instance types; expose tuning knobs for advanced customers.

High-level architecture options considered:
1) Data-parallel only: simplest but limited by single-GPU model size; not acceptable for 30B+ models without sharding.
2) Tensor-parallel (TP) only: shards linear layers across GPUs; reduces per-GPU memory for weights but needs efficient all-reduce for optimizer/activation aggregation (in our case activations/inputs).
3) Pipeline-parallel (PP) only: partition transformer blocks across devices to support very large models; introduces pipeline bubbles and micro-batching complexity.
4) Hybrid 2D (TP x PP): recommended for models >40B — use small TP group to shard large matmuls and use PP across blocks to scale depth.
We recommend starting with hybrid TPxPP for dedicated nodes, with configurable group sizes defaulting to TP=2 or 4 and PP chosen based on #layers and node count.

Topology & grouping:
- Grouping semantics: define an ordered pair (PP_rank, TP_rank) with global rank mapping. Groups used for NCCL collectives should be contiguous ranks when possible to leverage NVLink/NVML locality.
- Default mapping: colocate TP ranks on NVLink-connected GPUs to minimize PCIe/NVLink hops. For AWS/GCP instances with full NVLink mesh (8x A100), choose TP group inside the NVLink island.
- Host-level vs node-level: we prefer intra-node parallelism (NVLink) for TP and intra-rack NCCL tuning for PP communication between hosts.

NCCL tuning notes (practical defaults and rationale):
- NCCL_LAUNCH_MODE=PARALLEL: reduces kernel launch overhead on modern runtimes.
- NCCL_BUFFSIZE: tune per instance; use 8MB-32MB for high-latency networks, 1MB-8MB on NVLink-heavy topologies. Auto-config by detect of link type.
- NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0 / NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME: for RDMA-capable setups ensure IB enabled and proper interface binding. For noisy environments default to IB disabled and probe.
- NCCL_RING_THRESHOLD: lower threshold prevents huge ring all-reduces for small messages (helps low-latency inference).
- Use hierarchical all-reduce: intra-node NVLink collectives first, then inter-node via IB/NIC. This reduces cross-host traffic and improves latency.
- Timeout and recovery: increase NCCL_ASYNC_ERROR_HANDLING and set NCCL_TIMEOUT appropriately for large all-reduces; integrate with our watchdog to cancel stuck collectives.
- Logging: enable NCCL_DEBUG=INFO in debug builds; expose summary telemetry about bytes/collective durations to Console.

Sharding strategies (weights and KV cache):
Weights:
- TP sharding: split large linear layers along hidden dimension (column or row sharding depending on kernel). Use row-sharded bias terms as necessary.
- Sharded embedding/LMHead: use replicated or sharded depending on memory tradeoffs. For tokenizers with large vocab, prefer sharding.
- Checkpoint format: support serialized sharded checkpoints aligned to TP groups to avoid expensive redistribution at startup.

KV cache:
- Principle: KV cache must be low-latency access during decoding and as small as possible per-GPU.
- Sharding model: shard KV cache by TP dimension (i.e., each TP shard stores its local K/V for the tokens it is responsible for). For PP, the KV cache will also be distributed by pipeline stage; when a request moves across stages, only the stage-local KV slices are used.
- Addressing cross-stage dependency: for decoder-only models where later layers need full seq K/V, ensure each pipeline stage either holds its own K/V for its sub-layers OR we prefetch the necessary KV pieces over NCCL before attention. Prefetch should be batched to amortize latency.
- Eviction & LRU: implement per-GPU simple LRU by request-id/time to free memory for long-running sessions. Provide eviction hooks to front-end to return token-level progress if session is killed.
- Replication for fast failover: optionally maintain a replicated KV copy on a sibling GPU (same node) for critical sessions; this doubles KV memory but allows instant failover without re-computing keys. Make replication opt-in per-customer.

Kernel selection & operator optimizations:
- Support multiple attention kernels: flash-attn variants (fused kernels), causal streaming kernels, and fallback cuBLAS matmul paths. Select kernel based on: sequence length, batch size, dtype (fp16/int8), and GPU architecture.
- Attention bucketization: for very long sequences use blocked attention with windowed cache for recent context and efficient fallback to sparse or LRU-based retrieval.
- Quantized kernels: for quant profiles (int8/4-bit) use specialized GEMM kernels; ensure correctness tests (per-layer calibration).
- Workspace management: preallocate per-GPU workspaces for the largest supported layer to avoid dynamic allocations at runtime; track per-request allocs to prevent OOM.

Scheduling and batching model changes:
- Continuous batching pipeline: scheduler accepts tokens and forms micro-batches for PP fill/flush to reduce bubbles. Core concepts: micro-batch size (M), virtual batch for TP (V), and max tokens per batch.
- Micro-batching strategy: for PP choose M to fill pipeline stages without exceeding latency SLO. Use online profiling to pick M per-model and per-deployment.
- Adaptive batching: dynamic batch sizing driven by current queue depth and estimated service time; bias decisions by SLO-criticality header on requests.
- Priority and preemption: support SLO-based priorities — small low-latency requests can preempt large batches by reserving headroom in the next micro-batch. Implement preemption by fast-path single-GPU decode if needed.
- Scheduling across TP groups: ensure synchronized micro-batches across TP ranks; leader rank coordinates batch start. Use lightweight heartbeats to avoid deadlock.

Resource accounting and admission control:
- Estimate tokens*compute cost using perf table per model variant and adjust admission.
- Track per-GPU memory budget including model weights, KV, workspace, and expected batch footprint. Reject or redirect requests when memory headroom insufficient.

Failure modes and graceful degradation:
- NCCL collectives hang: detect via watchdog; abort collective and retry with reduced group size or fall back to replicated single-GPU path.
- OOM during decode: proactively reject/trim requests or evict low-priority KV cache entries.
- Pipeline-stage crash: if stage dies, attempt hot-restart on sibling GPU using checkpointed weights & optionally replicated KV. If restart not possible, rollback to a model variant with less parallelism.

Metrics and observability changes required:
- Per-collective stats: bytes transferred, duration, participants, topology map.
- KV cache metrics: per-GPU KV size, hit/miss rate, eviction counts, replication status.
- Pipeline metrics: bubble fraction, micro-batch occupancy, stage idle time.
- Kernel selection telemetry: which kernel was used, seq_len, batch_size, dtype, observed latency.

Benchmarks & experiments plan:
1) Baseline: single-node multi-GPU (8x A100) run for 7B/30B/65B models with TP=1..4, PP=1..8. Measure tokens/sec and p50/p95/p99 latency under synthetic workloads (flat and skewed seq_len patterns).
2) NCCL tuning matrix: test combinations of NCCL_BUFFSIZE, hierarchical allreduce vs flat, and IB enable/disable to choose defaults for common cloud providers.
3) KV eviction policy A/B: LRU-only vs time-window-first vs session-priority-first. Measure session success rate and tail latency.
4) Kernel selection thresholds: find breakpoints (seq_len, batch_size) where flash-attn outperforms fallback GEMM.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (lab): validate correctness for TPxPP hybrid with small clusters and CI tests (end-to-end decode correctness and deterministic output for deterministic seeds).
- Phase 1 (canary): offer as opt-in on Dedicated nodes; run low-volume production workloads and collect NCCL/kv/pipeline metrics.
- Phase 2 (gradual): enable for customers with >X throughput needs and monitor degradations; enable replication-based failover for critical sessions.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Default TP group size: conservative default 2 to keep all-reduces small; is this sufficient for typical 30B models? Need benchmark.
- KV replication cost vs failover benefit: quantify memory overhead per model size and decide default disabled.
- Prefetch complexity: how often do we pay prefetch cost vs keep local KV for every stage? Potential hybrid: prefetch only for cross-node PP boundaries.
- Checkpoint chunking: optimal shard size to balance startup time and storage overhead.

Action items / next steps:
- Ravi: implement hierarchical all-reduce proof-of-concept and perf harness (due 2026-01-15).
- Zoe: add KV cache telemetry & eviction hooks to runtime API (due 2026-01-30).
- Ethan: run kernel selection benchmarks for flash-attn vs cuBLAS across seq-lens (due 2026-02-10).
- Maya (owner): consolidate results and pick default TP/PP presets for Dedicated (due 2026-02-28).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: we prefer a conservative default that works across instance types and a set of advanced knobs for power users. Please focus review on failure modes and recovery strategies — those directly impact availability.
- Link to runtime PR with experimental TP/PP support: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/412

End of draft.
